title: Horizon Delivery: impairment of delivery drones under U.S. GAAP
participant_role: Financial reporting manager at Horizon Delivery finalizing year-end statements
judge_role: Lead external auditor who must confirm that Horizon's impairment testing follows U.S. GAAP

difficulty.rationale: The two-step impairment rule is given in the accounting manual, so students apply it to the numbers rather than recall ASC 360.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of financial reporting manager for HORIZON DELIVERY, a package delivery company. You are meeting with the lead external auditor (judge) to finalize the year-end financial statements.

Two years ago, Horizon Delivery bought a fleet of specialized delivery drones. The drones are carried on the balance sheet at a carrying value (book value) of $150,000. They have a remaining useful life of 4 years and no salvage value, and Horizon uses the straight-line depreciation method.

This year the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued strict new rules that restrict drone flights in suburban areas, sharply limiting how often Horizon can use the drones. The auditor (judge) considers this a triggering event and wants to see Horizon's impairment test. You have gathered the following estimates:

[Horizon drone fleet data: see exhibits]

The auditor (judge) needs to confirm that your work complies with U.S. GAAP (ASC 360, Property, Plant and Equipment).

Horizon's company accounting manual states: "Step 1 (recoverability): compare the carrying value with the total undiscounted future cash flows; if the cash flows are lower, the asset is impaired. Step 2 (measurement): impairment loss = carrying value minus fair value. The written-down value becomes the new basis for depreciation; U.S. GAAP does not allow the loss to be reversed later."

You must:
- Explain what an asset impairment is and why GAAP requires companies to test for it
- Apply Step 1 of the accounting manual to determine whether the drones are impaired
- Apply Step 2 of the accounting manual to calculate the amount of any impairment loss
- Prepare the journal entry to record the impairment
- Explain how the impairment affects this year's net income and next year's depreciation expense

You will present the information to the auditor (judge) in a role-play to take place in the auditor's (judge's) office. The auditor (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the auditor's (judge's) questions, the auditor (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: What if the estimated undiscounted future cash flows had been $160,000 instead of $140,000?
Our investors will see this loss next to our operating results. Where does it appear on the income statement, and does it use any cash?

solution.overview: A strong answer runs the two-step ASC 360 test: carrying value of $150,000 exceeds undiscounted cash flows of $140,000, so the drones are impaired, and the loss is measured against fair value: 150,000 minus 110,000 = $40,000. The presenter records the loss, shows next year's depreciation falls from $37,500 to $27,500, and notes that U.S. GAAP does not allow the loss to be reversed.

answer: An impairment is a drop in an asset's value so that its carrying value can no longer be recovered
Triggering events include new regulations, damage or falling demand; here, the FAA drone rules
GAAP requires the test so the balance sheet does not overstate assets (conservatism)
Compare carrying value $150,000 with undiscounted future cash flows $140,000
Cash flows are lower, so the carrying value is not recoverable
The drones are impaired; go to step 2
Loss = carrying value minus fair value
New carrying value (new cost basis): $110,000
Debit Impairment Loss $40,000
Credit Accumulated Depreciation, Drones $40,000
Reported in operating income on the income statement

by_task.task: Effect on net income and depreciation
answer: This year: pre-tax net income falls by the $40,000 loss
Next year before impairment: 150,000 / 4 = $37,500 depreciation
Next year after impairment: 110,000 / 4 = $27,500, which is $10,000 less each year
U.S. GAAP prohibits reversing the loss later even if value recovers (IFRS allows a reversal)

journal_entries.description: Record impairment of the drone fleet
Next year: straight-line depreciation on the new carrying value (110,000 / 4)

calculations.label: Step 1: recoverability test
steps: Carrying value $150,000 vs. undiscounted cash flows $140,000

judge_question_answers.question: What if the estimated undiscounted future cash flows had been $160,000 instead of $140,000?
answer: $160,000 of cash flows is more than the $150,000 carrying value, so the drones pass step 1
No impairment is recorded, even though fair value ($110,000) is lower
Depreciation would continue at $37,500 a year

judge_question_answers.question: Our investors will see this loss next to our operating results. Where does it appear on the income statement, and does it use any cash?
answer: It is reported as a separate line (impairment loss) within operating expenses on this year's income statement
It is a non-cash charge: no cash leaves the business when the drones are written down
On the statement of cash flows it is added back to net income in operating activities, like depreciation
Explain it to investors as a one-time effect of the new FAA rules, not a sign of weaker daily operations

tables.title: Record the impairment of the drone fleet
Next year: straight line depreciation on the new carrying value (110,000 / 4)

key_concepts.definition: A decline in a long-lived asset's value so that its carrying value cannot be recovered from future use or sale.
A change, such as new regulations or physical damage, that signals an asset may be impaired and must be tested.
Asset cost minus accumulated depreciation and any impairment losses.
Step 1 under ASC 360: the asset is impaired if its carrying value is greater than its undiscounted future cash flows.
Step 2 under ASC 360: impairment loss = carrying value minus fair value.
The price the asset could be sold for in an orderly transaction between market participants today.
The total cash an asset is expected to generate over its remaining life, without adjusting for the time value of money.
Depreciation = (carrying value minus salvage value) / remaining useful life, the same amount each year.
Once an impairment loss is recorded on an asset held and used, it cannot be reversed; IFRS allows a limited reversal.
When in doubt, accountants avoid overstating assets and income, so losses are recorded when they occur.

notes: State level impairment case; the accounting manual passage in the scenario gives the two-step rule, so the student is scored on applying it, and the remaining life and salvage value let students compute next year's depreciation. Watch for students who measure the loss against the $140,000 cash flows instead of the $110,000 fair value, or who say the loss can be reversed.

items.label: Discuss the nature of long-term assets

criteria.exceeds: Defines an impairment as a drop in value so the carrying value can no longer be recovered, names the FAA drone rules as the triggering event (along with examples like damage or falling demand), and explains that testing keeps the balance sheet from overstating assets (conservatism).
criteria.meets: Explains what an impairment is, identifies the FAA rules as the triggering event and states that the test keeps assets from being overstated.
criteria.below: Gives a vague definition of impairment or does not explain why the test is required.
criteria.little: Does not explain what an impairment is.

items.label: Describe the methods used to value long-term assets

criteria.exceeds: Applies both steps clearly: the $150,000 carrying value exceeds the $140,000 of undiscounted cash flows, so the drones are impaired; the loss is measured against fair value, 150,000 minus 110,000 = $40,000, leaving a new carrying value of $110,000, and explains why each step uses a different measure.
criteria.meets: Applies Step 1 to conclude the drones are impaired and Step 2 to calculate a $40,000 loss using the $110,000 fair value.
criteria.below: Gets Step 1 right but measures the loss against the $140,000 cash flows ($10,000), or skips Step 1.
criteria.little: Does not apply the test, or concludes the drones are not impaired.

criteria.exceeds: Records debit Impairment Loss $40,000, credit Accumulated Depreciation, Drones $40,000, and shows next year's depreciation entry of $27,500 (110,000 / 4) on the new carrying value.
criteria.meets: Records debit Impairment Loss $40,000 and credit Accumulated Depreciation (or the Drones asset account) $40,000.
criteria.below: Uses the right accounts with the wrong amount (such as $10,000), or reverses the debit and credit.
criteria.little: Gives no journal entry, or an entry with unrelated accounts.

criteria.exceeds: Explains that this year's pre-tax income falls by $40,000 while next year's depreciation drops from $37,500 to $27,500, $10,000 less each year for the remaining 4 years, and that the loss is a non-cash charge.
criteria.meets: States that net income falls by $40,000 this year and next year's depreciation becomes $27,500 instead of $37,500.
criteria.below: Describes only one of the effects, or gives wrong depreciation amounts.
criteria.little: Does not explain the effect on net income or depreciation.

items.label: Explain the nature of accounting standards

criteria.exceeds: Explains that U.S. GAAP (ASC 360) requires the two-step test, that the $110,000 becomes the new cost basis, and that U.S. GAAP prohibits reversing the loss even if value recovers, unlike IFRS, which allows a reversal.
criteria.meets: States that the test follows U.S. GAAP (ASC 360) and that the impairment loss cannot be reversed later under U.S. GAAP.
criteria.below: Mentions GAAP in general terms without connecting it to the test or the no reversal rule.
criteria.little: Does not mention accounting standards, or says the loss can be reversed next year.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the FAA rule to the test, the $40,000 loss, the new $110,000 basis and the lower depreciation in future years.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit data to the $40,000 impairment.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how one step affects the next.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the auditor a clear conclusion (record a $40,000 impairment now) and explains how to present it to investors as a one-time effect of the FAA rules.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear conclusion that a $40,000 impairment must be recorded.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a conclusion that is partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no conclusion, or says no impairment is needed.

criteria.exceeds: Walks the auditor through the test, entry and effects in a logical order with precise terms and confident, professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the test, calculation, entry and effects clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, mixes up terms like fair value and cash flows, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a simple visual or table ($150,000 carrying value against $140,000 cash flows and $110,000 fair value) that makes both steps obvious, and adds a useful idea such as how to explain the loss to investors.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the two-step test easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: with $160,000 of cash flows the drones pass Step 1, so no impairment is recorded even though fair value is $110,000 and depreciation stays at $37,500; and the loss is a separate line within operating expenses, is non-cash and is added back in operating activities on the cash flow statement.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that no impairment is recorded at $160,000 and that the loss uses no cash.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without numbers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says a loss is still recorded at $160,000 or that the loss uses cash.

key_points: The FAA rules are a triggering event; impairment testing keeps assets from being overstated
Step 1: carrying value $150,000 is greater than undiscounted cash flows $140,000, so the drones are impaired
Step 2: loss = $150,000 minus fair value $110,000 = $40,000; new carrying value $110,000
Entry: debit Impairment Loss $40,000, credit Accumulated Depreciation, Drones $40,000
This year's pre-tax income falls by $40,000; the loss is non-cash
Next year's depreciation falls from $37,500 (150,000 / 4) to $27,500 (110,000 / 4), $10,000 less per year
U.S. GAAP (ASC 360) does not allow the loss to be reversed; IFRS allows a reversal
